input.rationale: Interpreted the command-coverage receipt and fixed the harness omission it exposed. The result events show the same zero StoreConfiguration calls for all three dual-interface triggers (voter address change, AddNonvoter, RemoveServer) with 6, 6 and 5 ApplyBatch configuration entries and the control at 6 and 0, so the missing callback is not specific to one command; but the declared comparisons were unresolved because the setup event lacked the trigger field used as identity, so this update cites the result events for those values, records that limitation, and submits a corrected revision that adds the field to the setup event with the same cases and comparisons. No earlier receipt is withdrawn and no claim is weakened: the finding rests on the first two executions' satisfied comparisons plus these event values.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether an FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore still receives StoreConfiguration for a committed configuration change, as that interface documents, or only through ApplyBatch. The execution answers that it receives only ApplyBatch: in the dual-interface case the recorder shows 0 StoreConfiguration calls and 6 ApplyBatch configuration entries (parsed result event 3), while the ConfigurationStore-only control shows 6 and 0 (result event 1), with the setup events (0 and 2) matched as admissions and every comparison resolving. The source gives the mechanism: runFSM computes batchingEnabled once, and once it is true every batch goes to applyBatch, which forwards LogCommand and LogConfiguration entries to ApplyBatch and never calls StoreConfiguration; StoreConfiguration is reached only from applySingle, which the batched path does not use. What makes this a defect rather than a naming preference is the purpose the interface states for itself: storing configuration changes so that a persistent FSM state can behave as a complete snapshot and recover without an external one. An application that implements ConfigurationStore for that purpose, and also batches its applies for throughput, gets no callback and no error, so its durable state silently lacks the configuration it was promised. The scope is bounded and I record it plainly: the same entries do reach ApplyBatch, which BatchingFSM documents as receiving LogConfiguration, so an implementation that handles configuration changes in both places loses nothing observable, and the defect is the silent failure of the documented callback rather than lost information. A repeat of the same fixed experiment reproduced both counts exactly (receipt a5809ed4b5024b17adfebf093d3316f5, result events at parsed indices 1 and 3): the dual-interface FSM recorded 0 StoreConfiguration calls and 6 ApplyBatch configuration entries, the ConfigurationStore-only control recorded 6 and 0, and all four comparisons resolved as before. The account therefore rests on two executions rather than one, and the counts being identical across them is what makes the zero credible rather than an artifact of a single run's timing. A third execution covered other configuration commands and its result events carry the same shape (receipt f5bf67e282cb41c185854215b5b28e34, result events at parsed indices 1, 3, 5 and 7): the dual-interface FSM recorded 0 StoreConfiguration calls and 6, 6 and 5 ApplyBatch configuration entries after a voter address change, an AddNonvoter and a RemoveServer respectively, while the ConfigurationStore-only control recorded 6 and 0. Its declared comparisons came back unresolved rather than satisfied because the setup event did not carry the trigger field the identity used, so a corrected revision that adds that field to the setup event is submitted with this update; the values themselves are read from the result events, which carry the trigger and both counters. What the run adds is that the missing callback is not specific to one command: three different configuration changes produced the same zero.

knowledge.assertion: An FSM implementing both interfaces receives configuration changes only through ApplyBatch; two executions of the same probe recorded the same zero and six counts.

counterevidence: The configuration entry is not lost: BatchingFSM documents that ApplyBatch receives LogConfiguration entries, and the receipt shows all 6 deliveries there, so an application handling both paths is unaffected.

The combination is unusual rather than forbidden: nothing in either interface documents mutual exclusion, but an application that implements only one of them sees the documented behaviour, as the control case shows.
The trigger was a single configuration change (moving an existing voter's address); the same code path handles every LogConfiguration entry, but other change commands were not measured.
limitations: The command-coverage revision measured all three triggers with the dual-interface FSM and the control, but its declared comparisons were unresolved because the setup event did not carry the trigger field, so those values are cited from the result events rather than from satisfied comparisons; a corrected revision is submitted with this update.

The interactions are measured in two executions of the same fixed probe, which agree exactly (dual-interface FSM 0 StoreConfiguration calls and 6 ApplyBatch configuration entries; control 6 and 0), but both use three-voter clusters built by the repository's own helper with a shared recorder.
The consequence for an application's recovery is argued from the interface's stated purpose rather than demonstrated by recovering an FSM that missed the callback.

The change was triggered through AddVoter with a new address, AddNonvoter and RemoveServer; DemoteVoter and the deprecated Promote command were not measured.
interpretations.joint_history: Receipts 61281db3f55e4b03879ff0ae87c15000 and a5809ed4b5024b17adfebf093d3316f5 come from experiment 1995fd2023c948c99b650dce1b597cd6-experiment and receipt f5bf67e282cb41c185854215b5b28e34 from its revision 0c2ccd3e54bd41d385d13c33edaec69f-experiment. The revision kept the event names, the two interfaces, the counters and the control case, and changed only the commands that produce the configuration entry plus the trigger field; the first receipts therefore remain the satisfied-comparison evidence for the address-change case, while the later one supplies the command coverage whose comparisons were unresolved by a harness omission.

scope.description: Four cases as in the previous revision - a ConfigurationStore-only control and three dual-interface cases triggered by a voter address change, an AddNonvoter and a RemoveServer - each reporting the StoreConfiguration and ApplyBatch configuration counts, with the setup event now carrying the same trigger identifier as the result event so the admission can be matched.
assumptions: All three commands are legal on a three-voter cluster, as before.
The setup and result events now share batching_fsm and trigger, which is the identity the comparisons use.
The recorder is still shared across the cluster's FSMs.
excluded: DemoteVoter and the deprecated Promote command.

experiment.prefix: Each case calls MakeClusterCustom with three peers, bootstrapping and the in-memory test configuration, and a MakeFSMFunc returning either an FSM implementing FSM and ConfigurationStore or one that also implements ApplyBatch, all recording into a shared recorder. The case emits assurance_config_store_setup with the batching flag, the trigger name, the leader and target identities and the peer count, issues exactly one configuration command according to the trigger (AddVoter with a new address for the target voter, AddNonvoter for a fresh identity, or RemoveServer of the target follower), waits up to five seconds for a callback counter to become non-zero, waits a further 200ms, and emits assurance_config_store_result with the same trigger and batching flags plus the command's error and the counts. The harness is TestAssuranceConfigurationStoreWithBatching.

comparisons.description: Dual-interface FSM after an AddNonvoter: whether the documented callback arrives.
Dual-interface FSM after a RemoveServer: whether the documented callback arrives.
The standing dual-interface case, re-measured with the others.
Control: the ConfigurationStore-only FSM receives the callback.

experiment.revision_reason: The previous revision added two triggers but emitted the setup event without the trigger field, so the identity built from batching_fsm and trigger could not be matched and all four comparisons came back unresolved. This revision adds trigger to the setup event; cases, counters and comparisons are otherwise identical.

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits one CA_EVENT with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the quorum size, the leader term, the other servers' terms and states, the leader's state after the call, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport; the transports are fully connected before any node is started. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming all three as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, and the case waits until the leader's latest configuration reports the non-voter before proceeding. Configuration: HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, CommitTimeout = 5ms, default ProtocolVersion, which satisfies Config.Validate. After a 300ms settling period the transports are disconnected in both directions across the chosen boundary, so only the listed peers remain reachable from the leader; the observation then calls VerifyLeader() on the leader and reports nil, a concrete error, or pending after a 900ms wait. The peer kept reachable as a voter is chosen by position in the bootstrap configuration, and the non-voter by its join identity, never by a measured result.

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits a setup event with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the voter count, the quorum size and the reachable-peer flags, and a result event with the leader's state, term, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is added through the leader's AddNonvoter API rather than by constructing configuration state directly.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate.
Disconnecting both directions across the partition boundary models a network split rather than closing a node, so the leader keeps running and its lease timer still fires.
excluded: The stale-read half of the consequence: no successor election is expected to complete inside the observation window at these timeouts.

comparisons.description: Non-voter only reachable: the leader succeeds even though no other voter acknowledged. Holds means the predicted success was observed, which supports the defect account rather than contradicting it.
One voter reachable: positive control that a voter acknowledgement also produces success.
No peer reachable: control showing that success requires some acknowledged peer, so the non-voter-only success is not available to the leader on its own vote.

experiments.revision_reason: The previous harness emitted CA_EVENT objects without an event name, so the controller rejected all three as invalid_observation and no observation could be interpreted. This revision only changes the observation format: each case now emits a named assurance_partition_setup event before the partition and a named assurance_verify_leader_result event afterwards, carrying the same measured fields, and declares the setup event as a prerequisite admission with one comparison per partition case.

scope.description: Observe what LeadershipTransferToServer reports against which server actually takes leadership when the requested target is a non-voter, with the same call naming a voter as the only difference. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event describing the leader, the chosen target, its suffrage in the leader's latest configuration and the voter set, then an assurance_transfer_result event with the returned result, the target's and old leader's states, the leader set and terms after the call, and the time until any leader is observed.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; protocol version is the default (>= 3), so LeadershipTransferToServer is supported.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a real transfer rather than a probe that never succeeds.
excluded: Bounding the length of any leaderless interval: leadership state is sampled at the end of the 1500ms observation window, so this probe does not measure an interval.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts. Three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming them as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The target is then chosen by configuration role, never by a measured result: in the control case the first voter that is not the leader, in the probe case the joined non-voter; its suffrage is read back from the leader's latest configuration and reported in the setup event. The case calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.id, target.addr), waits up to 5s for the returned result, then waits up to 1500ms for the requested target to be observed as Leader and separately for any node to be Leader, and finally records the leader set, the maximum term across all four nodes and whether that term rose above the leader's term before the call. Both cases share the harness TestAssuranceLeadershipTransferTarget and are emitted under distinct case names.

comparisons.description: Non-voter target: what the call reported. Holds means the predicted success report was observed, which supports the defect account rather than contradicting it.
Non-voter target: the requested server never became leader within the observation window.
Voter target control: the same call does transfer leadership, so the non-voter outcome is not a probe that never transfers.
Voter target control: the reported result for a transfer that does complete.

scope.description: Observe both halves of a leadership transfer request naming a non-voter: what LeadershipTransferToServer reports, which server actually holds leadership, and how the cluster's leadership state evolves during the attempt, sampled every millisecond, with the same call naming a voter as the control. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event and an assurance_transfer_result event carrying the returned result, the target and previous-leader states, leader sets and terms, and the sampling counters.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate, and protocol version >= 3 supports LeadershipTransferToServer.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a completed transfer.

Sampling every millisecond is fine-grained relative to the 200ms election timeout, so a leaderless interval lasting an election round is expected to be visible; shorter gaps are not bounded by this sampling rate.
excluded: Process-level stalls, host suspends and multi-host clock behaviour, which a single-process in-memory probe does not reproduce.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process with their own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts. Three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The target is chosen by configuration role, never by a measured result: the first voter that is not the leader as the control, the joined non-voter as the probe; its suffrage is read from the leader's latest configuration and emitted in the setup event. The case calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.id, target.addr) and, from that instant, a goroutine samples every millisecond whether any of the four nodes is in Leader state and whether the previous leader is outside Leader state. It waits up to 5s for the returned result, up to 1500ms for the requested target to be observed as Leader, then records the leader set, the maximum term, whether the term rose above the pre-call term, and the sampling counters. Both cases share the harness TestAssuranceLeadershipTransferTarget under distinct case names.

Non-voter target: the previous leader was sampled outside Leader state during the attempt, so it did give up leadership.
Non-voter target: at least one sample found no leader in the cluster, with the first and last leaderless millisecond recorded alongside.
Voter target control: the same call does transfer leadership, so the non-voter outcome is not a probe that never transfers.
Voter target control: the reported result for a transfer that does complete.

experiments.revision_reason: The previous run of this harness answered the reported-result half of the question but sampled leadership state only at endpoints, so it could not say whether the cluster was ever without a leader or for how long. This revision adds a 1ms sampling goroutine running from the transfer call until after the observation window, reporting leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state, and the endpoint leader identity, with two comparisons asserting those observations for the non-voter case. Measured result fields, cases and target selection are unchanged.

scope.description: Run eight independent trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, arm a 600ms stall in the leader's log store, partition the leader so that only the non-voter remains reachable, drive a client Apply to block the leader's main loop on that store, queue VerifyLeader during the stall, and report the verify endpoint together with a 1ms leadership sampler over all four servers.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stalls; StoreLogs then blocks the leader's main loop, which is the goroutine that also serves the lease case and verify requests. The store is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; the stall is 600ms, three times the lease.
Only the elected leader's store is armed, so follower writes and their election timers behave as they would without the stall.
In-memory transports are used in one process, so RPC round trips are much faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: A leader blocked inside its own lease check rather than inside a store write, and host-level suspensions or clock jumps, which this probe does not reproduce.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store that wraps InmemStore and sleeps for 600ms inside StoreLogs while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster as Voter and the fourth node joins through the leader's own AddNonvoter call, with the trial waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The trial then emits assurance_stall_setup, disconnects the transports in both directions across the partition so that only the leader and the non-voter remain mutually reachable, starts a 1ms sampler that records every server's Leader state and the maximum term, arms the leader's stall, drives one Apply to make the leader write, queues VerifyLeader 300ms later, and reports assurance_stall_trial with the verify endpoint, the sample counters, the term reached, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyLeaderDuringLeaderStall.

comparisons.description: The stall was exercised and a different server was observed in Leader state at some point during or after it. Holds means the intended condition was reached.
Conditional on a successor having been observed: whether the queued VerifyLeader still reported success. Holds means the stale-read precondition was witnessed.
Restricted to trials where the stalled leader was never sampled outside Leader state: whether VerifyLeader reported success.

scope.description: Issue 64 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls in parallel against a freshly started single-voter node while Shutdown runs concurrently, count how many of those futures have not completed 400ms after Shutdown has returned, and compare with the same call kinds issued on a node that is never shut down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histogram and the shutdown error.
assumptions: A single-voter node is a supported configuration and makes each call complete quickly when the node is running, so any incomplete future is attributable to the shutdown race rather than to slow commit.
64 concurrent calls per trial is a probe of exposure, not a rate estimate; the concurrency is what makes the race observable.
Waiting 400ms after Shutdown() has returned is enough for any future that can still be answered, because the run loop has already exited by then.
excluded: Whether a stuck future can be recovered by any other API, and any multi-node variant where a future could still be answered by another goroutine after shutdown.

basis.prefix: Each case starts one real Raft instance in this process with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, bootstrapped as a single Voter with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms, and waits until it reports Leader. It then emits assurance_shutdown_setup and issues 64 calls of the chosen kind from separate goroutines, each waiting on Error() with a 1500ms local deadline and recording whether it returned and with which error. Concurrently, in the shutdown cases, Shutdown() is called and the case waits for it to return, then sleeps 400ms so that any future which can still be answered has been, and finally waits for all per-call timers before emitting assurance_shutdown_result with the returned and stuck counts, the outcome histogram, the shutdown error and the node state. The no-shutdown control issues the same calls without ever calling Shutdown. The harness is TestAssuranceShutdownFutureCompletion.

comparisons.description: VerifyLeader against a concurrent shutdown: at least one future never completed. Holds means the predicted hang was observed.
VerifyLeader control without shutdown: no future is left incomplete, so incompleteness is not a property of the probe itself.
Barrier against a concurrent shutdown: whether the same hang appears on the apply-channel path, which the harness drains in batches.
Apply against a concurrent shutdown: whether the same hang appears for command application.

scope.description: Six trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, register a VerifyLeader request at the leader while it is isolated from every peer, stall its main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms, then reconnect only the non-voter after 250 to 500ms and record the verify endpoint, when a different server was first sampled in Leader state, whether that preceded the verdict, the terms involved and the stall counters.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stall blocks its own main loop; it is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
Reconnecting the non-voter is a legal topology change: the transport is simply reconnected to a server that remains in the leader's latest configuration as a non-voter.

HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and a 900ms stall mean the leader's lease case cannot run during the stall while a voter majority can campaign at 200ms and elect a successor.
In-memory transports in one process, so RPC round trips are far faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: Multi-host clocks and process-level suspensions; and any case where the leader's own term is raised, since the partition keeps it at its old term.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process with their own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store whose StoreLogs sleeps 900ms while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The three voters are bootstrapped as Voter and the fourth node joins through the leader's AddNonvoter call. The trial emits assurance_registered_setup, disconnects the leader from both other voters and from the non-voter, calls VerifyLeader on the leader, waits 30ms so the main loop registers the request, arms the stall and drives one Apply so the leader's main loop blocks inside StoreLogs, starts a 1ms sampler over all four servers, then after the configured delay reconnects only the leader and the non-voter and waits for the verify future. It emits assurance_registered_result with the endpoint, the verdict time, whether another server was sampled in Leader state and when, the maximum term seen, the leader's term and state, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyRegisteredThenStalled.

scope.description: Five trials that each commit a value, partition and stall the leader, let a successor commit a different value, then compare the FSM values of the stalled leader and the successor after the leader's VerifyLeader returned, recording the verify endpoint, the two values, both terms and the stall counters.
assumptions: The mock FSM records each applied command in order, so its last value is what the node's state machine holds for that key; the harness reads it through the package's own test helper rather than by reaching into raft state.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The source trace shows the guarantee is weaker than that role requires: the confirming votes are gathered from every replication peer, including non-voters, while the threshold is a voter quorum. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus a single non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold and VerifyLeader returns nil; the same code gives the non-voter no standing in checkLeaderLease's lease count or in a vote request, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts. The consequence for reads is bounded rather than unconditional: checkLeaderLease uses voters only, so under a validated configuration the lease normally removes the old leader before a voter majority can elect a successor, and the acknowledgements counted while the leader is still legitimately leader are not themselves stale. The account therefore asserts a defect in the decision support VerifyLeader provides (success without voter-majority acknowledgement) and treats the stale-read consequence as conditional on the lease's timing assumption (a leader stall, clock jump or lease check interleaving that lets a successor be elected while the old leader still reports success). The requested probe fixes the acknowledging peer's identity independently of the result: the partition, not the outcome, selects the peer, and the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter path.
counterevidence: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, so a leader that has lost voter-majority contact steps down within about LeaderLeaseTimeout; this bounds the stale-read consequence rather than showing VerifyLeader's decision support to be adequate.

Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so a follower's election timer normally fires no earlier than the lease that causes the old leader to step down; the new-leader half of a stale read is therefore usually prevented by the lease rather than by the verify quorum.
limitations: The account is currently source-based; the three-case probe is requested with the recorded prediction that the non-voter-only partition returns success while the no-reachable-peer partition does not, and its retained receipt and parsed indices will be cited in a later update.
The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own replication and verify paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks.

The stale-read consequence requires a successor to be elected while the old leader still reports verify success (for example a leader stall or clock jump longer than ElectionTimeout - LeaderLeaseTimeout, or a verify request served before the ready lease case); no such condition has been observed yet.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM, and the question asks whether its success establishes the voter-majority contact that role implies. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly everywhere else: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter in its contacted tally, requestVote refuses a candidate that has no vote, and quorumSize itself counts voters only, so the verify path is the odd one out rather than a deliberate relaxation. interpretations.rationale: The documented purpose of LeadershipTransferToServer is to transition leadership to a specific server in the cluster, and the only target validation in the leader is a lookup in leaderState.replState, which holds an entry for every configured server except the leader regardless of Suffrage; a missing entry is the sole error. A non-voter therefore passes validation and is sent TimeoutNow, which makes it a Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer set, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote so the node sends a real RequestVote with a higher term. Voters processing that request adopt the higher term and set themselves to Follower before the hasVote check rejects the candidate, so the candidate cannot collect a single grant, while the old leader loses leadership because it adopts the higher term too and its transfer goroutine then reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch. The account is asserted on that source basis and stays conditional until the requested two-case probe reports what the call returns versus which server actually takes leadership; the controlling contrast is the same call naming a voter, and the note that auto-targeted LeadershipTransfer() skips non-voters via pickServer shows the library itself does not consider a non-voter a valid transfer target when it chooses.
counterevidence: The API does not state in its comment that the target must be a voter, and a caller who names only voters never reaches this path, so the defect depends on an accepted calling pattern rather than on the library's own choice of target.

LeadershipTransfer() without an explicit target filters non-voters in pickServer, which shows the intended transfer target set is the voter set and supports reading the targeted call as requiring the same premise.
A TimeoutNow that cannot be delivered (unreachable target) is reported as an error by the transfer path, so not every unusable target is silently accepted.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether LeadershipTransferToServer reports a transfer that the named server can complete when that server is a non-voter, and what happens to leadership while it cannot. The execution answers the first half directly. In the control case naming a voter (parsed indices 0 and 1) the call returned nil and the requested server was Leader at the endpoint while the previous leader was Follower, so the call does perform real transfers. In the case naming the non-voter (parsed indices 2 and 3, setup event index 2 matched as admission) the same call returned nil while the requested server was never observed as Leader within 1500ms and finished as Follower; the previous leader was not Leader at the endpoint and the maximum term across the cluster had risen from 2 to 4, with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a Raft leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The source explains the mechanism as predicted. The leader resolves the requested ID only through leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so a non-voter passes and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote, so it sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. Each voter adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before reaching the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote, so the requested server can never collect a grant. interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'.

The stale-read consequence needs a successor elected while the old leader reports verify success, and the two orderings that decide it are both in the source. A voter refuses a vote or a pre-vote while it still knows a leader other than the candidate (raft.go 1673-1679 and 1786-1792), and it clears that knowledge only in its own campaign path, which runs after HeartbeatTimeout without leader contact (raft.go 227-228). A successor therefore needs a quorum of voters that have already reached that trigger, so it cannot exist earlier than HeartbeatTimeout after their last contact with the old leader, plus the election rounds. The leader, meanwhile, steps down at the first lease check whose voter contact age exceeds LeaderLeaseTimeout, and ValidateConfig allows LeaderLeaseTimeout to equal HeartbeatTimeout: in the worst schedule the boundary check still counts the voter (the comparison is diff <= leaseTimeout) and the step-down follows after minCheckInterval = 10ms. interpretations.rationale: The question asked whether a leader stalled past its lease can still answer a queued VerifyLeader with success by counting the reachable non-voter, and the execution answers no for this model. In all eight trials (parsed result events at indices 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) the intended condition was reached: the stalled leader kept Leader state for every sample (leader_not_leader_samples 0 in seven trials and 1 in one) while a different server was observed in Leader state at term 3 between 345ms and 464ms after the partition, so the cluster really did have two servers believing they led it during the stall. The queued VerifyLeader nevertheless never reported success: every endpoint was non-nil, seven trials answering 'leadership lost while committing log' and two answering 'node is not the leader', all at 600-602ms, which is exactly when the 600ms store stall released the main loop. The same run's Apply in the same window also ended with ErrLeadershipLost. The endpoints distinguish the two interleavings: 'leadership lost while committing log' is the answer the leader loop's cleanup gives to a verify it has already registered, so in those trials the verify case was served and then the runLeader defer answered it when leadership was given up, while 'node is not the leader' is the follower loop's answer to a request still queued in verifyCh, so in those trials the request never even reached verifyLeader. Neither outcome counts the non-voter's acknowledgement. The reason is ordering rather than eligibility: by the time the stall ends, the lease case is already ready, so the main loop gives up leadership in the next iteration, before the heartbeat round trip to the non-voter can return a vote. limitations: One execution of eight trials is cited; the endpoints were uniform (0/8 success) but the reported interleavings are inferred from the two error values, not sampled directly.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown runs can be left permanently uncompleted, and the execution answers yes for VerifyLeader. In the retained run of three shutdown trials (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13) the verify cases left 9, 41 and 0 of their 64 futures uncompleted 400ms after Shutdown() had returned, with every completed call reporting success; the same call kind on a node that is never shut down completed all 64 in its control (index 19). So 50 of 192 verify calls were still waiting long after the node had reported Shutdown complete, and nothing is left that could answer them: Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets the state to Shutdown (api.go 1060-1072), the run loop and the FSM goroutine both exit on that channel, and the futures sit in verifyCh, a buffered channel of 64 (api.go 576) that nobody drains afterwards. That matches the source: VerifyLeader creates a verifyFuture and calls init(), which allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), leaving ShutdownCh nil, so deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117). The contract names ErrRaftShutdown as an error a client may see from these calls, and the repository's own test file already carries a TODO that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck when the buffered channel consumes a future that shutdown then never processes (raft_test.go 38-42). The exposure is timing dependent rather than uniform: the third verify trial left nothing behind, and the run's other two call kinds never left a future incomplete at all (Barrier 0 of 192 across indices 3, 9, 15; Apply 0 of 192 across 5, 11, 17). That difference is consistent with how the loop drains each channel: it takes one case per iteration from verifyCh, whereas applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries in the group-commit loop, so a queue of apply or barrier futures is emptied before the shutdown case is chosen far more reliably. The mechanism itself does not require many callers: any single VerifyLeader whose send wins the select while the loop is exiting lands in the buffer and stays there, but the likelihood that the buffer is non-empty at that moment grows with concurrent callers, which is what the probe exercises.
counterevidence: One of the three verify trials left no future uncompleted, and the two other call kinds never did in 384 attempts, so the outcome is a race whose probability depends on queue occupancy at the exit rather than a deterministic property of the API.

Every future that did complete in these trials reported success, so the hang is confined to calls that were never served; no completed call was answered with a wrong outcome.
limitations: The probe deliberately uses 64 concurrent VerifyLeader calls to make queue occupancy likely; it does not measure the probability for a single call racing Shutdown, only that the race exists.
The single-voter configuration removes commit latency as a confounder but also means verify requests need no peer round trip, so nothing else can be holding the queue.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and both retained runs say yes for VerifyLeader while excluding the other two. The first receipt adds the racing form of the same defect: with 64 calls issued just before Shutdown and a 1500ms wait, two of its three verify trials left 9 and 41 futures incomplete while the control left none (indices 1, 7, 13 and 19 there). The revision's racing phase left none, so that form is timing dependent; the post-shutdown form is not, and it is the one the account now rests on.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the revision: 0 of 128 calls per case were left incomplete, so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.

Barrier and Apply never stranded a future in either run (0 of 192 and 0 of 192 in the first receipt; 0 of 384 in the revision), which limits the defect to the VerifyLeader path unless BatchApplyCh is enabled.
Every call that was answered in these runs returned success or the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, so the defect is confined to calls whose future is never served.

interpretations.rationale: The question is whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and the corrected revision now answers it with all five declared comparisons satisfied, including the two that a configuration change makes decisive. A call made after Shutdown has returned should get the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, and that is what happens for the unbuffered call kinds: Barrier and Apply answered all eight post-shutdown calls in every trial (comparisons 2 and 3, indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17). VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered, answered only 4, 4 and 5 of its eight post-shutdown calls (indices 1, 7 and 13), leaving 4, 4 and 3 futures incomplete after 500ms. With BatchApplyCh enabled - the option whose comment says it buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries and thereby breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply - the two unbuffered kinds flip: Barrier answered 6, 3 and 4 of eight (indices 25, 29, 33) and Apply 3, 3 and 5 (indices 27, 31, 35), leaving 11 and 13 of 24 calls stranded respectively, with roughly half of the calls in each case answered and the rest left with a future nothing will complete (comparisons 0 and 1). That is a causal rather than correlational demonstration: the only difference between the answered and the stranded cases is whether the channel a future is sent to is buffered, since the call shape, the future type and the absence of a shutdown channel on these futures are identical. The source explains the split exactly: VerifyLeader and the apply path share the same select over the shutdown channel and a channel send, verifyCh is created with 64 slots while applyCh is unbuffered unless BatchApplyCh buffers it, and none of these futures sets ShutdownCh, so deferError.Error() waits on an error channel that no surviving goroutine will write. The repository's own test file records the same class as a TODO for these calls, which is an admission that the gap was known rather than a contract that permits a caller's Error() to block forever. The earlier receipts stay part of the account: the first showed the racing form, 9 and 41 of 64 futures incomplete in two of three trials with none in the control, and the two later revisions did not reproduce that form (0 of 128 per case), so the racing variant is a timing-dependent manifestation while the post-shutdown form is stable across three executions and is the one the claim rests on. A fifth revision tested whether the strand depends on spare capacity in verifyCh by issuing 320 concurrent racing calls, five times the 64 slots, in three VerifyLeader cases (result events at parsed indices 25, 27 and 29). Over-subscription did not protect later callers: 6, 5 and 6 of the eight post-shutdown calls were answered and 2, 3 and 2 returned futures that stayed incomplete, which is the same outcome as the 128-call cases in the same run (5, 1 and 3 answered; 3, 7 and 5 stranded) and the declared comparison asking for every post-shutdown call to be answered was therefore contradicted with three valid witnesses. The reading is that the racing surplus senders are released by the shutdown case instead of holding slots, so the buffer ends partially empty at the exit and later callers still find a free slot to be accepted into; occupancy at the exit is thus not what decides the strand, and the mechanism stands as the buffered channel plus a future with no shutdown channel of its own.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the later revisions (0 of 128 calls per case in two runs), so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.

Without BatchApplyCh the apply path is never affected: Barrier and Apply answered every post-shutdown call in all three runs (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17 here), so the defect reaches the apply path only under a configuration whose own comment already warns that it breaks the Apply timeout guarantee.

Roughly half of the calls in each affected case are answered with the documented shutdown error rather than stranded, so the outcome is a per-call select choice, and no call that was answered carried a wrong outcome.
The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO, which is evidence about intent, not a reason to treat an unbounded block as acceptable.

Over-subscribing verifyCh five-fold did not remove the strand: the 320-call cases stranded 2, 3 and 2 of eight post-shutdown calls, against 3, 7 and 5 of eight for the 128-call cases, so the outcome is not decided by spare capacity being available when the loop exits.
limitations: The post-shutdown counts per case come from three trials of eight calls each (VerifyLeader 11 of 24 stranded; batched Barrier 11 of 24; batched Apply 13 of 24), so they bound the mechanism rather than a population rate.
The strand is classified by a 500ms window; permanence is inferred from the source, since no reader of the affected channel remains and these futures carry no shutdown channel.
Single-voter node, in-memory transport, 50ms timeouts, one process: no peer round trip or networked shutdown is involved.

The over-subscribed cases carry 320 concurrent racing calls, five times the 64 verifyCh slots, so a large share of sends could not be accepted; the buffer still ended with free slots and the strand persisted, which means occupancy at the exit is not what the probe controls.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a follower can hold a committed configuration that was never committed and then truncate its log so that its latest configuration names a server with no entry behind it. The trace answers no for a leader that uses this library's configuration API, and the reason is the leader's own gate rather than the follower's care: configurationChangeChIfStable returns the change channel only while latestIndex equals committedIndex and the leader's commit index has reached the first entry of its term, so the library never lets a leader append a second configuration entry while the first is uncommitted. That makes processConfigurationLogEntry's shortcut - advancing the committed configuration to the previous latest one before installing the new entry - sound, because the previous latest configuration is precisely the one that must have committed for the new entry to exist. The follower's state can therefore read as committed while the follower's own commit index lags, but it does not name a configuration the cluster never committed. The truncation half is closed by geometry rather than by the shortcut: the fallback sets the latest configuration to the committed one at index I, and the truncation starts at the first conflicting index X where the follower's entry differs in term from the leader's. Entries below X are identical to the leader's, and a configuration that was genuinely committed must be present in the log of whichever server won the election afterwards, so X cannot be at or below I and the entry at I survives the DeleteRange. What would break this is a leader that appends two uncommitted configuration entries, which the gate above prevents in this implementation; I record that as the assumption the negative result rests on rather than as a second finding.
counterevidence: The negative result rests on the leader gate rather than on anything the follower verifies: a leader that wrote configuration entries outside that gate, or a log that already contained two uncommitted configurations, would make the shortcut unsound.

The appendEntries commit handling only advances the follower's committed configuration when the leader's commit index has reached its latest configuration index, so the follower's committed field can lag or lead its own commit index depending on which path set it last.
limitations: The account is source-based: no execution traced a follower through an append of a configuration entry, a withheld commit and a forced truncation, so the reasoning about index ordering is not measured.
The argument about identical entries below the conflict index relies on Raft's log-matching property rather than on an observation in this snapshot.
It covers the library's own configuration API and does not consider a user writing LogConfiguration entries into the log directly.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'. The consequence that this account previously kept conditional is now witnessed. A separate probe registers the verify request while the leader is isolated from every peer, stalls the leader's main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so its lease case cannot run, and reconnects only the non-voter once a voter majority has had time to elect. In all six trials a different server was sampled in Leader state at term 3 before the verdict (first at 319-454ms) while the old leader stayed at term 2, and in three of them (result events at parsed indices 3, 7 and 9) the old leader's VerifyLeader returned success at 931ms - the moment the stall released the loop, by which time the non-voter's acknowledgement had already been counted on a replication goroutine. The other three trials answered 'leadership lost while committing log', so the outcome is a per-trial choice between the two ready cases, but the successful ones are exactly the stale-read verdict the API says it prevents: a caller told 'still leader' while a successor already led at a higher term. Two details keep this from contradicting the earlier refuted child question, which asked whether a request *queued during* the stall can succeed: it cannot, because the main loop must be running to register the request, and that is why the successful construction registers first and stalls afterwards. The parent defect claim is unchanged; what changes is its consequence, which is no longer conditional on an unobserved interleaving but demonstrated under a stated condition. The repeat of that probe strengthens the witness rather than merely confirming it: in the second run (receipt 2f645950e0334342b1f7392ed1c1f286, result events at parsed indices 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11) the successor overlap again appeared in all six trials, with a different server first sampled in Leader state at term 3 between 345ms and 511ms while the old leader stayed at term 2, and five of the six trials returned VerifyLeader success at 931-932ms - only the 250ms reconnection answered 'leadership lost while committing log'. Across the two runs the overlap holds in twelve of twelve trials and success in eight of twelve, so what reproduces is the overlap, while the verdict itself remains a per-trial choice between the ready verify case and the ready lease case. The account, its defect claim and its resolved gap answer are otherwise unchanged. The last limitation this account carried is now closed by a probe that reads the FSM instead of inferring the consequence. Each trial commits the value 'old' through the leader and waits for it to reach every node, partitions the leader, stalls its main loop, lets a successor at term 3 commit the value 'new', reconnects only the non-voter, and then reads the mock FSM on both nodes after the verify returns. All five trials show the divergence the consequence needs: the stalled leader's FSM still held 'old' while the successor held 'new' (comparisons at parsed indices 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, the latter two confirming the successor's value), and in the two trials where the verify returned success (indices 1 and 7, reconnections 300ms and 450ms) a caller following the documented pattern would have read 'old' from a node it had just been told was still the leader, while the cluster's state was 'new'. The other three trials answered 'leadership lost while committing log', so the read only matters when the verify succeeds; the verdict remains the per-trial choice recorded earlier.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether an FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore still receives StoreConfiguration for a committed configuration change, as that interface documents, or only through ApplyBatch. The execution answers that it receives only ApplyBatch: in the dual-interface case the recorder shows 0 StoreConfiguration calls and 6 ApplyBatch configuration entries (parsed result event 3), while the ConfigurationStore-only control shows 6 and 0 (result event 1), with the setup events (0 and 2) matched as admissions and every comparison resolving. The source gives the mechanism: runFSM computes batchingEnabled once, and once it is true every batch goes to applyBatch, which forwards LogCommand and LogConfiguration entries to ApplyBatch and never calls StoreConfiguration; StoreConfiguration is reached only from applySingle, which the batched path does not use. What makes this a defect rather than a naming preference is the purpose the interface states for itself: storing configuration changes so that a persistent FSM state can behave as a complete snapshot and recover without an external one. An application that implements ConfigurationStore for that purpose, and also batches its applies for throughput, gets no callback and no error, so its durable state silently lacks the configuration it was promised. The scope is bounded and I record it plainly: the same entries do reach ApplyBatch, which BatchingFSM documents as receiving LogConfiguration, so an implementation that handles configuration changes in both places loses nothing observable, and the defect is the silent failure of the documented callback rather than lost information.
counterevidence: The configuration entry is not lost: BatchingFSM documents that ApplyBatch receives LogConfiguration entries, and the receipt shows all 6 deliveries there, so an application handling both paths is unaffected.

The combination is unusual rather than forbidden: nothing in either interface documents mutual exclusion, but an application that implements only one of them sees the documented behaviour, as the control case shows.
The trigger was a single configuration change (moving an existing voter's address); the same code path handles every LogConfiguration entry, but other change commands were not measured.
limitations: One execution with two cases, three voters each, using the repository's own cluster helper; the recorder was shared across the cluster's FSMs, so the counts show that the callback is never invoked anywhere rather than per node.
The change was triggered through AddVoter with a new address for an existing voter, which is a legal change but not the AddNonvoter or RemoveServer paths.
The consequence for an application's recovery is argued from the interface's stated purpose rather than demonstrated by recovering an FSM that missed the callback.

result.summary: Interpreted the command-coverage receipt and repaired the harness omission it exposed. The result events show the same zero StoreConfiguration calls for all three dual-interface triggers — a voter address change, an AddNonvoter and a RemoveServer — with 6, 6 and 5 ApplyBatch configuration entries and the ConfigurationStore-only control at 6 and 0, so the missing callback is not specific to one command; the declared comparisons came back unresolved because the setup event did not carry the trigger field used as identity, so I cited the result events for those values, recorded that as a limitation, and submitted a corrected revision that adds the field with the same cases and comparisons. The account's earlier satisfied comparisons and receipts are unchanged and the finding is not weakened, and joint history explains how the two experiments' receipts compose. About twenty-five minutes of run time remain; the outstanding item is interpreting the corrected revision's receipt, and if the run ends before it arrives the request stands as a fixed experiment with its prediction recorded.

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits one CA_EVENT with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the quorum size, the leader term, the other servers' terms and states, the leader's state after the call, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport; the transports are fully connected before any node is started. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming all three as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, and the case waits until the leader's latest configuration reports the non-voter before proceeding. Configuration: HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, CommitTimeout = 5ms, default ProtocolVersion, which satisfies Config.Validate. After a 300ms settling period the transports are disconnected in both directions across the chosen boundary, so only the listed peers remain reachable from the leader; the observation then calls VerifyLeader() on the leader and reports nil, a concrete error, or pending after a 900ms wait. The peer kept reachable as a voter is chosen by position in the bootstrap configuration, and the non-voter by its join identity, never by a measured result.

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits a setup event with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the voter count, the quorum size and the reachable-peer flags, and a result event with the leader's state, term, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is added through the leader's AddNonvoter API rather than by constructing configuration state directly.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate.
Disconnecting both directions across the partition boundary models a network split rather than closing a node, so the leader keeps running and its lease timer still fires.
excluded: The stale-read half of the consequence: no successor election is expected to complete inside the observation window at these timeouts.

experiments.revision_reason: The previous harness emitted CA_EVENT objects without an event name, so the controller rejected all three as invalid_observation and no observation could be interpreted. scope.description: Observe what LeadershipTransferToServer reports against which server actually takes leadership when the requested target is a non-voter, with the same call naming a voter as the only difference. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event describing the leader, the chosen target, its suffrage in the leader's latest configuration and the voter set, then an assurance_transfer_result event with the returned result, the target's and old leader's states, the leader set and terms after the call, and the time until any leader is observed.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; protocol version is the default (>= 3), so LeadershipTransferToServer is supported.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a real transfer rather than a probe that never succeeds.
excluded: Bounding the length of any leaderless interval: leadership state is sampled at the end of the 1500ms observation window, so this probe does not measure an interval.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts. Three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming them as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The target is then chosen by configuration role, never by a measured result: in the control case the first voter that is not the leader, in the probe case the joined non-voter; its suffrage is read back from the leader's latest configuration and reported in the setup event. The case calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.id, target.addr), waits up to 5s for the returned result, then waits up to 1500ms for the requested target to be observed as Leader and separately for any node to be Leader, and finally records the leader set, the maximum term across all four nodes and whether that term rose above the leader's term before the call. Both cases share the harness TestAssuranceLeadershipTransferTarget and are emitted under distinct case names.

Voter target control: the same call does transfer leadership, so the non-voter outcome is not a probe that never transfers.
Voter target control: the reported result for a transfer that does complete.

scope.description: Observe both halves of a leadership transfer request naming a non-voter: what LeadershipTransferToServer reports, which server actually holds leadership, and how the cluster's leadership state evolves during the attempt, sampled every millisecond, with the same call naming a voter as the control. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event and an assurance_transfer_result event carrying the returned result, the target and previous-leader states, leader sets and terms, and the sampling counters.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate, and protocol version >= 3 supports LeadershipTransferToServer.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a completed transfer.

Sampling every millisecond is fine-grained relative to the 200ms election timeout, so a leaderless interval lasting an election round is expected to be visible; shorter gaps are not bounded by this sampling rate.
excluded: Process-level stalls, host suspends and multi-host clock behaviour, which a single-process in-memory probe does not reproduce.
