experiments.revision_reason: The previous run of this harness answered the reported-result half of the question but sampled leadership state only at endpoints, so it could not say whether the cluster was ever without a leader or for how long. This revision adds a 1ms sampling goroutine running from the transfer call until after the observation window, reporting leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state, and the endpoint leader identity, with two comparisons asserting those observations for the non-voter case. Measured result fields, cases and target selection are unchanged.

scope.description: Run eight independent trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, arm a 600ms stall in the leader's log store, partition the leader so that only the non-voter remains reachable, drive a client Apply to block the leader's main loop on that store, queue VerifyLeader during the stall, and report the verify endpoint together with a 1ms leadership sampler over all four servers.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stalls; StoreLogs then blocks the leader's main loop, which is the goroutine that also serves the lease case and verify requests. The store is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; the stall is 600ms, three times the lease.
Only the elected leader's store is armed, so follower writes and their election timers behave as they would without the stall.
In-memory transports are used in one process, so RPC round trips are much faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: A leader blocked inside its own lease check rather than inside a store write, and host-level suspensions or clock jumps, which this probe does not reproduce.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store that wraps InmemStore and sleeps for 600ms inside StoreLogs while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster as Voter and the fourth node joins through the leader's own AddNonvoter call, with the trial waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The trial then emits assurance_stall_setup, disconnects the transports in both directions across the partition so that only the leader and the non-voter remain mutually reachable, starts a 1ms sampler that records every server's Leader state and the maximum term, arms the leader's stall, drives one Apply to make the leader write, queues VerifyLeader 300ms later, and reports assurance_stall_trial with the verify endpoint, the sample counters, the term reached, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyLeaderDuringLeaderStall.

comparisons.description: The stall was exercised and a different server was observed in Leader state at some point during or after it. Holds means the intended condition was reached.
Conditional on a successor having been observed: whether the queued VerifyLeader still reported success. Holds means the stale-read precondition was witnessed.
Restricted to trials where the stalled leader was never sampled outside Leader state: whether VerifyLeader reported success.

scope.description: Issue 64 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls in parallel against a freshly started single-voter node while Shutdown runs concurrently, count how many of those futures have not completed 400ms after Shutdown has returned, and compare with the same call kinds issued on a node that is never shut down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histogram and the shutdown error.
assumptions: A single-voter node is a supported configuration and makes each call complete quickly when the node is running, so any incomplete future is attributable to the shutdown race rather than to slow commit.
64 concurrent calls per trial is a probe of exposure, not a rate estimate; the concurrency is what makes the race observable.
Waiting 400ms after Shutdown() has returned is enough for any future that can still be answered, because the run loop has already exited by then.
excluded: Whether a stuck future can be recovered by any other API, and any multi-node variant where a future could still be answered by another goroutine after shutdown.

basis.prefix: Each case starts one real Raft instance in this process with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, bootstrapped as a single Voter with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms, and waits until it reports Leader. It then emits assurance_shutdown_setup and issues 64 calls of the chosen kind from separate goroutines, each waiting on Error() with a 1500ms local deadline and recording whether it returned and with which error. Concurrently, in the shutdown cases, Shutdown() is called and the case waits for it to return, then sleeps 400ms so that any future which can still be answered has been, and finally waits for all per-call timers before emitting assurance_shutdown_result with the returned and stuck counts, the outcome histogram, the shutdown error and the node state. The no-shutdown control issues the same calls without ever calling Shutdown. The harness is TestAssuranceShutdownFutureCompletion.

comparisons.description: VerifyLeader against a concurrent shutdown: at least one future never completed. Holds means the predicted hang was observed.
VerifyLeader control without shutdown: no future is left incomplete, so incompleteness is not a property of the probe itself.
Barrier against a concurrent shutdown: whether the same hang appears on the apply-channel path, which the harness drains in batches.
Apply against a concurrent shutdown: whether the same hang appears for command application.

scope.description: In three trials per call kind, issue 128 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls while Shutdown is interleaved into the fill, count how many of those futures are still incomplete 4000ms later, then issue 8 further calls of the same kind after Shutdown has returned and record whether each is answered within 500ms; a no-shutdown control runs the same call kinds without ever shutting down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histograms for both phases and the shutdown error.
assumptions: VerifyLeader is a legal call at any time, including after Shutdown, and the documented generic error for that case is ErrRaftShutdown, which the API's own select returns when the shutdown channel is chosen.
A single-voter node removes commit latency as a confounder and makes every call complete in well under a millisecond while the node is running.
The 4000ms window is long enough that a future answered only by the exited run loop would show as incomplete; nothing else in the harness can answer these futures.
excluded: A BatchApplyCh configuration, where applyCh becomes buffered and the apply path should behave like the verify path; and multi-node variants.

The no-shutdown control never calls Shutdown. The harness is TestAssuranceShutdownFutureCompletion.

comparisons.description: VerifyLeader after Shutdown returned: at least one of the eight post-shutdown calls was still unanswered after 500ms. Holds means the predicted strand was observed on a call that has no race with the shutdown itself.
Barrier after Shutdown returned: the contrast case, expected to answer every post-shutdown call with the shutdown error because its channel is unbuffered by default.
Apply after Shutdown returned: same contrast as Barrier.
VerifyLeader control without shutdown: no call is left incomplete when nothing is shutting down.

experiments.revision_reason: The first run left the trigger timing dependent (9, 41 and 0 stranded futures across three trials) and waited only 1500ms per call, so the revision lengthens the completion window to 4000ms, raises the call count to 128, interleaves Shutdown 2ms into the fill, and adds a post-shutdown phase that issues 8 calls of the same kind after Shutdown has returned and records which of them are answered promptly. No measured field was removed and the event names are unchanged.

scope.description: Run the shutdown probe for VerifyLeader, Barrier and Apply with the default unbuffered applyCh and again for Barrier and Apply with BatchApplyCh enabled, three trials each, recording how many futures are left incomplete in the racing phase and how many of eight post-shutdown calls are answered in the 500ms window, plus a no-shutdown control.
assumptions: BatchApplyCh is a supported configuration option whose documented effect is to buffer applyCh to MaxAppendEntries and to break the timeout guarantee on Apply.
Buffer size is MaxAppendEntries (the default), which is large enough that the eight post-shutdown sends never block, so the send case is selectable exactly as verifyCh's is.
Single-voter node, in-memory transport, 50ms timeouts, one process, as before.
excluded: BatchApplyCh with BatchApplyChMaxAppendEntries or concurrency large enough to fill the buffer, and multi-node behaviour.

basis.prefix: Each case starts one real Raft instance with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, bootstrapped as a single Voter with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms and BatchApplyCh set only for the batched cases, and waits until it reports Leader. It emits assurance_shutdown_setup with the batch_apply_ch flag, issues 128 calls of the chosen kind from separate goroutines, each waiting on Error() with a 4000ms deadline, and in the shutdown cases calls Shutdown() from a goroutine 2ms later so the fill and the exit overlap. After Shutdown returns it issues 8 further calls of the same kind one at a time with a 500ms wait each, then emits assurance_shutdown_result with the racing counts, the post-phase counts and histograms, the shutdown error, the node state and the batch_apply_ch flag. The no-shutdown control never calls Shutdown. The harness is TestAssuranceShutdownFutureCompletion.

comparisons.description: Barrier with BatchApplyCh: at least one of eight post-shutdown calls left unanswered, which would show the strand follows the buffering rather than the API.
Apply with BatchApplyCh: same prediction for the documented buffered configuration.
Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh: every post-shutdown call answered, the contrast that the batched case is measured against.
Apply with the default unbuffered applyCh: same contrast.

scope.description: Six trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, register a VerifyLeader request at the leader while it is isolated from every peer, stall its main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms, then reconnect only the non-voter after 250 to 500ms and record the verify endpoint, when a different server was first sampled in Leader state, whether that preceded the verdict, the terms involved and the stall counters.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stall blocks its own main loop; it is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
Reconnecting the non-voter is a legal topology change: the transport is simply reconnected to a server that remains in the leader's latest configuration as a non-voter.

HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and a 900ms stall mean the leader's lease case cannot run during the stall while a voter majority can campaign at 200ms and elect a successor.
In-memory transports in one process, so RPC round trips are far faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: Multi-host clocks and process-level suspensions; and any case where the leader's own term is raised, since the partition keeps it at its old term.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process with their own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store whose StoreLogs sleeps 900ms while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The trial emits assurance_registered_setup, disconnects the leader from both other voters and from the non-voter, calls VerifyLeader on the leader, waits 30ms so the main loop registers the request, arms the stall and drives one Apply so the leader's main loop blocks inside StoreLogs, starts a 1ms sampler over all four servers, then after the configured delay reconnects only the leader and the non-voter and waits for the verify future. It emits assurance_registered_result with the endpoint, the verdict time, whether another server was sampled in Leader state and when, the maximum term seen, the leader's term and state, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyRegisteredThenStalled.

comparisons.description: The stalled leader returned VerifyLeader success even though it could reach no voter for the whole window.

scope.description: Five trials that each commit a value, partition and stall the leader, let a successor commit a different value, then compare the FSM values of the stalled leader and the successor after the leader's VerifyLeader returned, recording the verify endpoint, the two values, both terms and the stall counters.
assumptions: The mock FSM records each applied command in order, so its last value is what the node's state machine holds for that key; the harness reads it through the package's own test helper rather than by reaching into raft state.
The value committed before the partition has reached every node, checked by waiting after the apply, so the two nodes start from the same state.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, a 900ms store stall that blocks the leader's main loop, and in-memory transports in one process.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances of the same shape as the earlier witness probe: three voters bootstrapped as Voter and one non-voter joined through the leader's AddNonvoter call, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, and only the elected leader's log store armed with a 900ms stall. The stalled leader's own FSM never advanced past the value committed before the partition.
The successor committed the different value, so the cluster did move on while the old leader was stalled.

This revision keeps the same build, partition, stall and reconnection and adds committed values: a value applied and replicated before the partition, a different value applied by the successor afterwards, and reads of the mock FSM on both nodes after the verify returns. scope.description: Two cases, each a three-voter cluster built with the repository's own cluster helper whose FSMs share a recorder: one case where the FSM implements FSM and ConfigurationStore, and one where it also implements BatchingFSM. Each case triggers a single configuration change by moving an existing voter's address, waits until the change reaches the FSM, and reports how many times StoreConfiguration and ApplyBatch were called with configuration entries.
assumptions: Moving an existing voter's address is a legal configuration change that nextConfiguration accepts for a voter, and with three voters the entry commits on the leader and one other node before the moved address matters.
The recorder is shared across the cluster's FSMs only to answer whether the callback is ever invoked anywhere in the cluster; per-node attribution is not needed for that question.
The cluster helper builds in-memory transports and stores, so no external service is involved.
excluded: Whether an application should rely on StoreConfiguration when it also batches, and any behaviour of ApplyBatch ordering or responses.

basis.prefix: Each case calls MakeClusterCustom with three peers, bootstrapping and the in-memory test configuration, and a MakeFSMFunc that returns either an FSM implementing FSM and ConfigurationStore or one that also implements ApplyBatch; both record every callback into a shared recorder. The case emits assurance_config_store_setup, picks a follower, calls leader.AddVoter with that follower's ID and a new address (so that the configuration changes without removing anyone), waits up to five seconds for either callback counter to become non-zero, waits a further 200ms, and emits assurance_config_store_result with the call counts. The harness is TestAssuranceConfigurationStoreWithBatching.

comparisons.description: An FSM implementing both interfaces: whether the documented StoreConfiguration callback arrives for a committed configuration change.
The same case: whether the configuration entry was delivered through ApplyBatch instead.
Control: an FSM implementing only ConfigurationStore does receive the callback, so the difference is the batching interface and not the trigger.
Control: the non-batching FSM sees no ApplyBatch call at all.

scope.description: Four cases, each a three-voter cluster built with the repository's own helper whose FSMs share a recorder: a ConfigurationStore-only FSM with a voter address change as the control, and three dual-interface FSMs whose single configuration change is a voter address change, an AddNonvoter, or a RemoveServer of a follower. Each case reports the StoreConfiguration and ApplyBatch configuration counts together with the command's result.
assumptions: All three commands are legal on a three-voter cluster: moving a voter's address keeps three voters, AddNonvoter adds a non-voter, and removing one follower leaves two voters, which is still a quorum.
Each case produces exactly one committed configuration entry, so the counts are comparable across cases.
As before, the recorder is shared across the cluster's FSMs so the counts answer whether the callback fires anywhere.
excluded: DemoteVoter and the deprecated Promote/AddStaging commands, and any multi-command sequence.

basis.prefix: Each case calls MakeClusterCustom with three peers, bootstrapping and the in-memory test configuration, and a MakeFSMFunc returning either an FSM implementing FSM and ConfigurationStore or one that also implements ApplyBatch, all recording into a shared recorder. The case emits assurance_config_store_setup with the batching flag, the trigger name, the leader and target identities and the peer count, then issues exactly one configuration command according to the trigger: AddVoter with a new address for the target voter, AddNonvoter for a fresh address-based identity, or RemoveServer of the target follower. interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The source trace shows the guarantee is weaker than that role requires: the confirming votes are gathered from every replication peer, including non-voters, while the threshold is a voter quorum. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus a single non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold and VerifyLeader returns nil; the same code gives the non-voter no standing in checkLeaderLease's lease count or in a vote request, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts. The consequence for reads is bounded rather than unconditional: checkLeaderLease uses voters only, so under a validated configuration the lease normally removes the old leader before a voter majority can elect a successor, and the acknowledgements counted while the leader is still legitimately leader are not themselves stale. The account therefore asserts a defect in the decision support VerifyLeader provides (success without voter-majority acknowledgement) and treats the stale-read consequence as conditional on the lease's timing assumption (a leader stall, clock jump or lease check interleaving that lets a successor be elected while the old leader still reports success). The requested probe fixes the acknowledging peer's identity independently of the result: the partition, not the outcome, selects the peer, and the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter path.
counterevidence: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, so a leader that has lost voter-majority contact steps down within about LeaderLeaseTimeout; this bounds the stale-read consequence rather than showing VerifyLeader's decision support to be adequate.

Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so a follower's election timer normally fires no earlier than the lease that causes the old leader to step down; the new-leader half of a stale read is therefore usually prevented by the lease rather than by the verify quorum.
limitations: The account is currently source-based; the three-case probe is requested with the recorded prediction that the non-voter-only partition returns success while the no-reachable-peer partition does not, and its retained receipt and parsed indices will be cited in a later update.
The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own replication and verify paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks.

The stale-read consequence requires a successor to be elected while the old leader still reports verify success (for example a leader stall or clock jump longer than ElectionTimeout - LeaderLeaseTimeout, or a verify request served before the ready lease case); no such condition has been observed yet.

interpretations.rationale: The documented purpose of LeadershipTransferToServer is to transition leadership to a specific server in the cluster, and the only target validation in the leader is a lookup in leaderState.replState, which holds an entry for every configured server except the leader regardless of Suffrage; a missing entry is the sole error. A non-voter therefore passes validation and is sent TimeoutNow, which makes it a Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer set, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote so the node sends a real RequestVote with a higher term. Voters processing that request adopt the higher term and set themselves to Follower before the hasVote check rejects the candidate, so the candidate cannot collect a single grant, while the old leader loses leadership because it adopts the higher term too and its transfer goroutine then reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch. The account is asserted on that source basis and stays conditional until the requested two-case probe reports what the call returns versus which server actually takes leadership; the controlling contrast is the same call naming a voter, and the note that auto-targeted LeadershipTransfer() skips non-voters via pickServer shows the library itself does not consider a non-voter a valid transfer target when it chooses.
counterevidence: The API does not state in its comment that the target must be a voter, and a caller who names only voters never reaches this path, so the defect depends on an accepted calling pattern rather than on the library's own choice of target.

LeadershipTransfer() without an explicit target filters non-voters in pickServer, which shows the intended transfer target set is the voter set and supports reading the targeted call as requiring the same premise.
A TimeoutNow that cannot be delivered (unreachable target) is reported as an error by the transfer path, so not every unusable target is silently accepted.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether LeadershipTransferToServer reports a transfer that the named server can complete when that server is a non-voter, and what happens to leadership while it cannot. The execution answers the first half directly. In the control case naming a voter (parsed indices 0 and 1) the call returned nil and the requested server was Leader at the endpoint while the previous leader was Follower, so the call does perform real transfers. In the case naming the non-voter (parsed indices 2 and 3, setup event index 2 matched as admission) the same call returned nil while the requested server was never observed as Leader within 1500ms and finished as Follower; the previous leader was not Leader at the endpoint and the maximum term across the cluster had risen from 2 to 4, with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a Raft leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The source explains the mechanism as predicted. The leader resolves the requested ID only through leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so a non-voter passes and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote, so it sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. Each voter adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before reaching the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote, so the requested server can never collect a grant. The old leader learns of the higher term, steps down, and its transfer goroutine reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch, so the caller is told the transfer succeeded while leadership has in fact left it for a server it did not choose, or returned to it in a later term. That mismatch is the defect: for the documented purpose of handing leadership over, a success result that the named target can never satisfy leaves the caller unable to distinguish a completed handover from a self-inflicted leadership interruption. The liveness side is bounded rather than unbounded and this receipt does not measure it, since leadership was sampled only at the end of the observation window; the revised probe samples every millisecond and records the leaderless samples. No data loss is claimed: committed entries stay committed and a voter is elected afterwards.

That mismatch is the defect: the documented purpose of the call is to hand leadership to the named server, and a success result that the named server can never satisfy leaves the caller unable to distinguish a completed handover from a self-inflicted interruption that costs the cluster the leaderless interval it takes to elect someone else. No data loss is claimed: committed entries stay committed, and the control case shows the probe does observe a completed transfer.

627b3ef0c6e049bfb836e40ffbdce875-gap-1.explanation: Resolved by the revised probe (receipt 23acf06d8a524b2790ef674d5eb04cb0). In the non-voter case (result event index 3) the previous leader was outside Leader state in every one of the 1289 samples taken from the instant of the call, and at least one sample found no leader in the cluster: 241 of those samples were leaderless, the first at 1ms and the last at 278ms after the call, so with a 200ms election timeout the cluster was observed without a leader for about 277ms, roughly 1.4 election timeouts, while the requested target never held leadership and the maximum term rose from 2 to 4 with a different voter holding leadership at the end. interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'.

d704b04e706144dc964ff451359eda19-gap-0.explanation: Still unresolved, but now bounded from both sides. The grant side closes what the previous answer left open: a voter rejects a vote request while it still knows a leader other than the candidate (raft.go 1673-1679, and the same check on pre-votes at 1786-1792) and clears that knowledge only when its own campaign path runs, which requires HeartbeatTimeout without leader contact (raft.go 227-228). What remains untested is whether that residual is reachable at all, and whether a stalled leader goroutine widens it, so the gap stays open as a schedule-dependent condition rather than a configuration-dependent one.

interpretations.rationale: The question asked whether a leader stalled past its lease can still answer a queued VerifyLeader with success by counting the reachable non-voter, and the execution answers no for this model. In all eight trials (parsed result events at indices 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) the intended condition was reached: the stalled leader kept Leader state for every sample (leader_not_leader_samples 0 in seven trials and 1 in one) while a different server was observed in Leader state at term 3 between 345ms and 464ms after the partition, so the cluster really did have two servers believing they led it during the stall. The queued VerifyLeader nevertheless never reported success: every endpoint was non-nil, seven trials answering 'leadership lost while committing log' and two answering 'node is not the leader', all at 600-602ms, which is exactly when the 600ms store stall released the main loop. The same run's Apply in the same window also ended with ErrLeadershipLost. The endpoints distinguish the two interleavings: 'leadership lost while committing log' is the answer the leader loop's cleanup gives to a verify it has already registered, so in those trials the verify case was served and then the runLeader defer answered it when leadership was given up, while 'node is not the leader' is the follower loop's answer to a request still queued in verifyCh, so in those trials the request never even reached verifyLeader. Neither outcome counts the non-voter's acknowledgement. The reason is ordering rather than eligibility: by the time the stall ends, the lease case is already ready, so the main loop gives up leadership in the next iteration, before the heartbeat round trip to the non-voter can return a vote. This refutes the suspicion for this route, not the parent defect: the accounting behaviour that counts a non-voter remains in the source and was observed directly in the parent question's probe. What the trial excludes is the specific consequence I was probing, namely that a stalled leader serving a queued verify hands a client a stale-read verdict. Two limits keep that exclusion narrow: it was measured with in-memory transports, where the acknowledgement round trip is far faster than the loop iteration that gives up leadership, and at eight trials it cannot bound an interleaving whose window is sub-millisecond. The parent question's gap therefore narrows to that scheduling residue rather than closing.
counterevidence: The stall model, not the source, is what the trials refute: a slower or differently placed stall could change which case the main loop serves first, and a networked deployment makes each RPC round trip orders of magnitude slower than the loop iteration, which is the opposite direction from the one that produced these endpoints.

In two trials the failure was ErrNotLeader rather than ErrLeadershipLost, showing the queued request sometimes never reached verifyLeader at all; those trials measure the queue being drained after leadership loss rather than the race between the acknowledgement and the step-down.
limitations: One execution of eight trials is cited; the endpoints were uniform (0/8 success) but the reported interleavings are inferred from the two error values, not sampled directly.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'.

Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, and ReloadConfig re-runs ValidateConfig, so a leader cannot be configured to outlive a follower's election timer through the public reload API.

In the non-voter partition the other servers stayed in term 2 with no leader change, so the receipt does not witness a successor being elected while the old leader still verified; that half of the consequence remains unobserved.

The grant side bounds the consequence more tightly than the verify quorum does: because a voter refuses votes while it knows another leader, no successor can be elected before HeartbeatTimeout plus an election round after the last leader contact, while the lease removes the old leader at LeaderLeaseTimeout + minCheckInterval at the latest; with the documented defaults the two cannot overlap, and even when LeaderLeaseTimeout equals HeartbeatTimeout the residual is a few milliseconds.

The stale-read consequence needs a successor elected while the old leader reports verify success, and the two orderings that decide it are both in the source. interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown runs can be left permanently uncompleted, and the execution answers yes for VerifyLeader. In the retained run of three shutdown trials (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13) the verify cases left 9, 41 and 0 of their 64 futures uncompleted 400ms after Shutdown() had returned, with every completed call reporting success; the same call kind on a node that is never shut down completed all 64 in its control (index 19). So 50 of 192 verify calls were still waiting long after the node had reported Shutdown complete, and nothing is left that could answer them: Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets the state to Shutdown (api.go 1060-1072), the run loop and the FSM goroutine both exit on that channel, and the futures sit in verifyCh, a buffered channel of 64 (api.go 576) that nobody drains afterwards. That matches the source: VerifyLeader creates a verifyFuture and calls init(), which allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), leaving ShutdownCh nil, so deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117). The contract names ErrRaftShutdown as an error a client may see from these calls, and the repository's own test file already carries a TODO that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck when the buffered channel consumes a future that shutdown then never processes (raft_test.go 38-42). The exposure is timing dependent rather than uniform: the third verify trial left nothing behind, and the run's other two call kinds never left a future incomplete at all (Barrier 0 of 192 across indices 3, 9, 15; Apply 0 of 192 across 5, 11, 17). That difference is consistent with how the loop drains each channel: it takes one case per iteration from verifyCh, whereas applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries in the group-commit loop, so a queue of apply or barrier futures is emptied before the shutdown case is chosen far more reliably. The mechanism itself does not require many callers: any single VerifyLeader whose send wins the select while the loop is exiting lands in the buffer and stays there, but the likelihood that the buffer is non-empty at that moment grows with concurrent callers, which is what the probe exercises.
counterevidence: One of the three verify trials left no future uncompleted, and the two other call kinds never did in 384 attempts, so the outcome is a race whose probability depends on queue occupancy at the exit rather than a deterministic property of the API.

The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO for Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration, which is a source admission that the gap exists rather than a contract that permits it; it is cited here as evidence about intent, not as a reason to withhold the finding.
Every future that did complete in these trials reported success, so the hang is confined to calls that were never served; no completed call was answered with a wrong outcome.
limitations: The probe deliberately uses 64 concurrent VerifyLeader calls to make queue occupancy likely; it does not measure the probability for a single call racing Shutdown, only that the race exists.
The single-voter configuration removes commit latency as a confounder but also means verify requests need no peer round trip, so nothing else can be holding the queue.

Whether a stuck future could ever be answered later is inferred from the source and from the node reporting Shutdown complete with no loop running; the harness waited 1500ms per call and 400ms after Shutdown returned, not indefinitely.

Barrier and Apply never stranded a future in either run (0 of 192 and 0 of 192 in the first receipt; 0 of 384 in the revision), which limits the defect to the VerifyLeader path unless BatchApplyCh is enabled.
Every call that was answered in these runs returned success or the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, so the defect is confined to calls whose future is never served.

d704b04e706144dc964ff451359eda19-gap-0.explanation: Resolved. The legal condition is a leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease while a non-voter it can reach becomes reachable during the stall: configuration routes are not needed. The new probe registered a VerifyLeader request while the leader was isolated from every peer, blocked its main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so the lease case could not fire, and reconnected only the non-voter after 250-500ms. In all six trials a successor was sampled in Leader state at term 3 before the verdict (first at 319-454ms) with the old leader still at term 2; in three trials the verify returned success at 931ms, when the stall released the loop and the already-counted non-voter vote was delivered, and the other three answered leadership loss. The earlier bound still explains normal operation: without a stall the lease case is always ready by the time a successor can exist, so the two cannot overlap; the stall is what removes that protection, because the lease check runs on the main loop.

knowledge.assertion: A leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease can return VerifyLeader success after a non-voter's acknowledgement is counted during the stall, even though a successor led at a higher term for the whole interval.

counterevidence: The leadership lease still bounds the ordinary case: without a stalled main loop the lease case is served no later than LeaderLeaseTimeout, which is why the six-trial probe needed a 900ms store stall to reach the condition.

Only three of the six trials returned success; the other three answered leadership loss, so the verdict is a per-trial choice between the ready verify case and the ready lease case rather than a deterministic outcome.

The witness depends on a non-voter in the configuration and reachable from the stalled leader; the earlier controls show that without any acknowledgement the same call fails (no-peer control) and that a voter acknowledgement is the legitimate path.
The stalled leader never adopted the successor's term (leader_term_after stayed 2 in every trial), which is what makes the two leaders coexist and the verdict stale.
limitations: The stall is a wrapper around the log store that blocks StoreLogs on the leader's main thread, and the non-voter is reconnected by transport calls; both are supplied conditions rather than faults observed in a deployment.

The verdict arrives when the stall releases the main loop (931-932ms in every trial), so the success is returned at the first loop iteration after the acknowledgement had already been counted, not while the loop was blocked.

The caller's subsequent read of the FSM is not exercised; the stale-read consequence is that the API's documented purpose ('to prevent returning stale data from the FSM') is not met, which the witness establishes from the endpoint and the concurrent successor rather than from a data read.

Experiment 29a71a7377a44fdbac949d4808f7b847-experiment (receipt 01617c5662f34c3eb21857602f6cac4f) reuses that build and adds the stall, the isolated registration and the late non-voter reconnection. interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'. The consequence that this account previously kept conditional is now witnessed. A separate probe registers the verify request while the leader is isolated from every peer, stalls the leader's main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so its lease case cannot run, and reconnects only the non-voter once a voter majority has had time to elect. In all six trials a different server was sampled in Leader state at term 3 before the verdict (first at 319-454ms) while the old leader stayed at term 2, and in three of them (result events at parsed indices 3, 7 and 9) the old leader's VerifyLeader returned success at 931ms - the moment the stall released the loop, by which time the non-voter's acknowledgement had already been counted on a replication goroutine. The other three trials answered 'leadership lost while committing log', so the outcome is a per-trial choice between the two ready cases, but the successful ones are exactly the stale-read verdict the API says it prevents: a caller told 'still leader' while a successor already led at a higher term. Two details keep this from contradicting the earlier refuted child question, which asked whether a request *queued during* the stall can succeed: it cannot, because the main loop must be running to register the request, and that is why the successful construction registers first and stalls afterwards. The parent defect claim is unchanged; what changes is its consequence, which is no longer conditional on an unobserved interleaving but demonstrated under a stated condition.

d704b04e706144dc964ff451359eda19-gap-0.explanation: Resolved. The legal condition is a leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease while a non-voter it can reach becomes reachable during the stall: configuration routes are not needed. The new probe registered a VerifyLeader request while the leader was isolated from every peer, blocked its main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so the lease case could not fire, and reconnected only the non-voter after 250-500ms. In all six trials a successor was sampled in Leader state at term 3 before the verdict (first at 319-454ms) with the old leader still at term 2; in three trials the verify returned success at 931ms, when the stall released the loop and the already-counted non-voter vote was delivered, and the other three answered leadership loss. The earlier bound still explains normal operation: without a stall the lease case is always ready by the time a successor can exist, so the two cannot overlap; the stall is what removes that protection, because the lease check runs on the main loop.

knowledge.assertion: Election vote solicitation asks only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so the verify path's inclusion of non-voters is an omission rather than the intended eligibility rule.
A follower campaigns after HeartbeatTimeout without leader contact, not after ElectionTimeout, and the leader's lease check granularity is max(10ms, LeaderLeaseTimeout - maxDiff).

A leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease can return VerifyLeader success after a non-voter's acknowledgement is counted during the stall, even though a successor led at a higher term for the whole interval.

counterevidence: The leadership lease still bounds the ordinary case: without a stalled main loop the lease case is served no later than LeaderLeaseTimeout, which is why the six-trial probe needed a 900ms store stall to reach the condition.

Only three of the six trials returned success; the other three answered leadership loss, so the verdict is a per-trial choice between the ready verify case and the ready lease case rather than a deterministic outcome.

The witness depends on a non-voter in the configuration and reachable from the stalled leader; the earlier controls show that without any acknowledgement the same call fails (no-peer control) and that a voter acknowledgement is the legitimate path.
The stalled leader never adopted the successor's term (leader_term_after stayed 2 in every trial), which is what makes the two leaders coexist and the verdict stale.
limitations: The stall is a wrapper around the log store that blocks StoreLogs on the leader's main thread, and the non-voter is reconnected by transport calls; both are supplied conditions rather than faults observed in a deployment.

The verdict arrives when the stall releases the main loop (931-932ms in every trial), so the success is returned at the first loop iteration after the acknowledgement had already been counted, not while the loop was blocked.

The caller's subsequent read of the FSM is not exercised; the stale-read consequence is that the API's documented purpose ('to prevent returning stale data from the FSM') is not met, which the witness establishes from the endpoint and the concurrent successor rather than from a data read.
In-memory transports in one process with 200ms timeouts and a 900ms stall; multi-host clocks and process suspensions are not covered.

interpretations.rationale: The question is whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and the corrected revision now answers it with all five declared comparisons satisfied, including the two that a configuration change makes decisive. A call made after Shutdown has returned should get the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, and that is what happens for the unbuffered call kinds: Barrier and Apply answered all eight post-shutdown calls in every trial (comparisons 2 and 3, indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17). VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered, answered only 4, 4 and 5 of its eight post-shutdown calls (indices 1, 7 and 13), leaving 4, 4 and 3 futures incomplete after 500ms. With BatchApplyCh enabled - the option whose comment says it buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries and thereby breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply - the two unbuffered kinds flip: Barrier answered 6, 3 and 4 of eight (indices 25, 29, 33) and Apply 3, 3 and 5 (indices 27, 31, 35), leaving 11 and 13 of 24 calls stranded respectively, with roughly half of the calls in each case answered and the rest left with a future nothing will complete (comparisons 0 and 1). That is a causal rather than correlational demonstration: the only difference between the answered and the stranded cases is whether the channel a future is sent to is buffered, since the call shape, the future type and the absence of a shutdown channel on these futures are identical. The source explains the split exactly: VerifyLeader and the apply path share the same select over the shutdown channel and a channel send, verifyCh is created with 64 slots while applyCh is unbuffered unless BatchApplyCh buffers it, and none of these futures sets ShutdownCh, so deferError.Error() waits on an error channel that no surviving goroutine will write. The repository's own test file records the same class as a TODO for these calls, which is an admission that the gap was known rather than a contract that permits a caller's Error() to block forever. The earlier receipts stay part of the account: the first showed the racing form, 9 and 41 of 64 futures incomplete in two of three trials with none in the control, and the two later revisions did not reproduce that form (0 of 128 per case), so the racing variant is a timing-dependent manifestation while the post-shutdown form is stable across three executions and is the one the claim rests on. A fifth revision tested whether the strand depends on spare capacity in verifyCh by issuing 320 concurrent racing calls, five times the 64 slots, in three VerifyLeader cases (result events at parsed indices 25, 27 and 29). Over-subscription did not protect later callers: 6, 5 and 6 of the eight post-shutdown calls were answered and 2, 3 and 2 returned futures that stayed incomplete, which is the same outcome as the 128-call cases in the same run (5, 1 and 3 answered; 3, 7 and 5 stranded) and the declared comparison asking for every post-shutdown call to be answered was therefore contradicted with three valid witnesses. The reading is that the racing surplus senders are released by the shutdown case instead of holding slots, so the buffer ends partially empty at the exit and later callers still find a free slot to be accepted into; occupancy at the exit is thus not what decides the strand, and the mechanism stands as the buffered channel plus a future with no shutdown channel of its own.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the later revisions (0 of 128 calls per case in two runs), so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.

Without BatchApplyCh the apply path is never affected: Barrier and Apply answered every post-shutdown call in all three runs (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17 here), so the defect reaches the apply path only under a configuration whose own comment already warns that it breaks the Apply timeout guarantee.

Roughly half of the calls in each affected case are answered with the documented shutdown error rather than stranded, so the outcome is a per-call select choice, and no call that was answered carried a wrong outcome.
The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO, which is evidence about intent, not a reason to treat an unbounded block as acceptable.

Over-subscribing verifyCh five-fold did not remove the strand: the 320-call cases stranded 2, 3 and 2 of eight post-shutdown calls, against 3, 7 and 5 of eight for the 128-call cases, so the outcome is not decided by spare capacity being available when the loop exits.
limitations: The post-shutdown counts per case come from three trials of eight calls each (VerifyLeader 11 of 24 stranded; batched Barrier 11 of 24; batched Apply 13 of 24), so they bound the mechanism rather than a population rate.
The strand is classified by a 500ms window; permanence is inferred from the source, since no reader of the affected channel remains and these futures carry no shutdown channel.
Single-voter node, in-memory transport, 50ms timeouts, one process: no peer round trip or networked shutdown is involved.

The over-subscribed cases carry 320 concurrent racing calls, five times the 64 verifyCh slots, so a large share of sends could not be accepted; the buffer still ended with free slots and the strand persisted, which means occupancy at the exit is not what the probe controls.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a follower can hold a committed configuration that was never committed and then truncate its log so that its latest configuration names a server with no entry behind it. The trace answers no for a leader that uses this library's configuration API, and the reason is the leader's own gate rather than the follower's care: configurationChangeChIfStable returns the change channel only while latestIndex equals committedIndex and the leader's commit index has reached the first entry of its term, so the library never lets a leader append a second configuration entry while the first is uncommitted. That makes processConfigurationLogEntry's shortcut - advancing the committed configuration to the previous latest one before installing the new entry - sound, because the previous latest configuration is precisely the one that must have committed for the new entry to exist. The follower's state can therefore read as committed while the follower's own commit index lags, but it does not name a configuration the cluster never committed. The truncation half is closed by geometry rather than by the shortcut: the fallback sets the latest configuration to the committed one at index I, and the truncation starts at the first conflicting index X where the follower's entry differs in term from the leader's. Entries below X are identical to the leader's, and a configuration that was genuinely committed must be present in the log of whichever server won the election afterwards, so X cannot be at or below I and the entry at I survives the DeleteRange. What would break this is a leader that appends two uncommitted configuration entries, which the gate above prevents in this implementation; I record that as the assumption the negative result rests on rather than as a second finding.
counterevidence: The negative result rests on the leader gate rather than on anything the follower verifies: a leader that wrote configuration entries outside that gate, or a log that already contained two uncommitted configurations, would make the shortcut unsound.

The appendEntries commit handling only advances the follower's committed configuration when the leader's commit index has reached its latest configuration index, so the follower's committed field can lag or lead its own commit index depending on which path set it last.
limitations: The account is source-based: no execution traced a follower through an append of a configuration entry, a withheld commit and a forced truncation, so the reasoning about index ordering is not measured.
The argument about identical entries below the conflict index relies on Raft's log-matching property rather than on an observation in this snapshot.
It covers the library's own configuration API and does not consider a user writing LogConfiguration entries into the log directly.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether an FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore still receives StoreConfiguration for a committed configuration change, as that interface documents, or only through ApplyBatch. The execution answers that it receives only ApplyBatch: in the dual-interface case the recorder shows 0 StoreConfiguration calls and 6 ApplyBatch configuration entries (parsed result event 3), while the ConfigurationStore-only control shows 6 and 0 (result event 1), with the setup events (0 and 2) matched as admissions and every comparison resolving. The source gives the mechanism: runFSM computes batchingEnabled once, and once it is true every batch goes to applyBatch, which forwards LogCommand and LogConfiguration entries to ApplyBatch and never calls StoreConfiguration; StoreConfiguration is reached only from applySingle, which the batched path does not use. What makes this a defect rather than a naming preference is the purpose the interface states for itself: storing configuration changes so that a persistent FSM state can behave as a complete snapshot and recover without an external one. An application that implements ConfigurationStore for that purpose, and also batches its applies for throughput, gets no callback and no error, so its durable state silently lacks the configuration it was promised. The scope is bounded and I record it plainly: the same entries do reach ApplyBatch, which BatchingFSM documents as receiving LogConfiguration, so an implementation that handles configuration changes in both places loses nothing observable, and the defect is the silent failure of the documented callback rather than lost information.
counterevidence: The configuration entry is not lost: BatchingFSM documents that ApplyBatch receives LogConfiguration entries, and the receipt shows all 6 deliveries there, so an application handling both paths is unaffected.

The combination is unusual rather than forbidden: nothing in either interface documents mutual exclusion, but an application that implements only one of them sees the documented behaviour, as the control case shows.
The trigger was a single configuration change (moving an existing voter's address); the same code path handles every LogConfiguration entry, but other change commands were not measured.
limitations: One execution with two cases, three voters each, using the repository's own cluster helper; the recorder was shared across the cluster's FSMs, so the counts show that the callback is never invoked anywhere rather than per node.
The change was triggered through AddVoter with a new address for an existing voter, which is a legal change but not the AddNonvoter or RemoveServer paths.
The consequence for an application's recovery is argued from the interface's stated purpose rather than demonstrated by recovering an FSM that missed the callback.
